task_title: Course Development, Lesson Plans, and Classroom Training Techniques
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the teaching process, course and lesson design, every delivery method and instructional aid the FAA describes, and use them to write and teach a classroom ground lesson and a maneuver introduction lesson that fit the Task and the learner.
why: The FAA says success as an instructor depends largely on organizing material and choosing a method that fits the lesson [[25:125|AIH 5-22]]. On the CFI checkride you will be asked to explain these ideas and to prepare a lesson plan with methods and materials suited to the Task and the learner, so this lesson gives you both the theory and a working format.

key_terms.def: Four steps that organize material so learners can understand it: preparation, presentation, application and assessment [[25:104|AIH 5-1]].
A complete series of studies leading to a specific goal, such as a certificate [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].
A step-by-step, building-block progression of learning with regular review and assessments at set stages [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].
An organized, written outline for a single instructional period: what to do, in what order and by what procedure [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].
A measurable objective with a description of the skill or behavior, conditions and criteria [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].
An objective designed to develop judgment and ADM, suited to scenario-based training [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].
A test item is content valid when the maneuver mimics actual flying, and criterion valid when its completion standards reflect acceptable standards [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].
Measurable units of learning that combine, like a pyramid, to meet the overall training objective [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].
An instructor-controlled discussion that uses questions to draw out what learners know and check their understanding [[25:116|AIH 5-13]] [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].
Lessons that involve learners with real-life problems and ask them to find real-world solutions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].
A device that supports, supplements or reinforces what is taught; it is not self-supporting [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].
Teaching maneuvers by both outside visual references and flight instruments from the first time each is introduced [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

chunks.title: Teaching: the process and the essential skills

body.p: Teaching is to instruct or train. The AIH quotes psychologist Stanford Ericksen: good teachers select and organize worthwhile material, help learners encode it in a form they will remember, make sure they are competent in the procedures of the discipline, keep their curiosity alive, and teach them how to learn on their own [[25:104|AIH 5-1]].

Process. The teaching process organizes what you want to teach so the learner can understand it. It has four steps: preparation, presentation, application and assessment. Whatever delivery method you use, the sequence stays the same [[25:104|AIH 5-1]].

head: Step
What happens
What it looks like for a CFI
rows: Preparation
Objectives and standards are set before any instruction. A syllabus gives you the starting objectives [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]
Write the lesson objective and completion standards, then the plan [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]
Presentation
Deliver the lesson with a method that fits it, and keep the learners' attention [[25:111|AIH 5-8]] [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]
Lecture, discussion, demonstration or a mix [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]
Application
The learner uses the material: explains it in class, or performs the maneuver you just demonstrated. Your explanation and demonstration alternate with the learner's tries [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]
Correct early, because the learner needs to do it right the first few times to build a good habit [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]
Assessment
Before the period ends, review what was covered and have the learners show how well the objectives were met. It can be informal or formal and recorded [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]
Use it to plan the next lesson [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]

callout.text: Chapter 7 names the same four steps for a lesson plan as preparation, presentation, application, and review and evaluation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

body.p: Essential skills. The AIH lists four essential skills that good teachers have: people skills, subject matter expertise, management skills and assessment skills [[25:104|AIH 5-1]].

head: Essential skill
What it means
In your lessons
rows: People skills
Effective communication. Technical knowledge is useless if you cannot get it across, and good communication includes actively listening [[25:105|AIH 5-2]]
Interact respectfully, notice when learners are not following, motivate, adapt, challenge them while supporting them, and show enthusiasm [[25:105|AIH 5-2]]
Subject matter expertise
A subject matter expert (SME) has a high level of knowledge or skill in an area [[25:105|AIH 5-2]]
Stay a lifelong learner: FAA seminars, conventions, professional groups, online classes, observing and being mentored by other instructors [[25:105|AIH 5-2]]
Management skills
The ability to plan, organize, lead and supervise; for an instructor, to plan, organize and carry out a lesson and manage its time [[25:105|AIH 5-2]]
Plan time for the unexpected and do not plan too much for the time you have [[25:105|AIH 5-2]]. Supervise, for example by overseeing the preflight so tasks are done correctly [[25:106|AIH 5-3]]
Assessment skills
Learning is a change in behavior, so it can be measured. Assessments can be made before, during and after training [[25:106|AIH 5-3]]
Decide what each assessment is for before you give it [[25:106|AIH 5-3]]

callout.text: The AIH's model instructor, Bob, arrives 30 minutes early to check the room, his notes, the computer and the handouts, so he is free to greet learners when they walk in [[25:104|AIH 5-1]]. That is management skill in action [[25:105|AIH 5-2]].

check.q: Your lesson went smoothly, but you never checked whether the learners met the objective. Which step of the teaching process did you skip?
check.a: Assessment. Before the period ends you should review and have the learners show how well the objectives were met [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

body.p: A course of training is a complete series of studies leading to a specific goal, such as a certificate of completion, graduation or a degree. A private pilot certificate course is one; so is something as narrow as the extra training for high-performance airplanes [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].
Three related terms sit inside it [[25:107|AIH 5-4]]:

bullets: Curriculum: for pilot training it usually includes courses for the various certificates and ratings [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].

Syllabus: a summary or outline of one course that contains multiple lessons, with a description of each lesson, its objectives and completion standards. A training syllabus is a step-by-step, building-block progression with regular review and assessments at set stages [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].
Lesson plan: a detailed plan for one lesson: objectives, organization of the material, teaching aids, instructor and learner actions, evaluation criteria and completion standards [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].

body.p: You plan the content of a course by setting its objectives and standards. Those in turn decide the lesson plans, test items and levels of learning [[25:145|AIH 7-1]]. Much of the basic planning is already given to you by the knowledge and proficiency requirements in 14 CFR part 61, approved school syllabi and published texts [[25:145|AIH 7-1]].

callout.text: Part 61 sets minimum experience and knowledge but does not say how training is organized. That flexibility lets you tailor lessons, but an instructor who does not organize the training can cost a learner time and money through repetitious training; a well-documented syllabus prevents it [[1:34|PHAK 1-19]]. The PHAK also says the learner should know in advance what the course involves and the criteria for completing it, with a briefing and debriefing every lesson [[1:38|PHAK 1-23]].

check.q: What is the difference between a syllabus and a lesson plan?
check.a: A syllabus outlines a whole course of many lessons with each lesson's objectives and completion standards. A lesson plan is the detailed plan for one lesson, including organization, aids, instructor and learner actions and completion standards [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].

chunks.title: Preparing a lesson: objectives, standards and the ACS

body.p: Objectives and standards come before instruction. Many instructors use a commercially developed syllabus, and its objectives are your starting point [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

Training objectives and completion standards. Aviation training uses two types of objectives: performance-based and decision-based [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Objectives apply to all three domains of learning and should state the level of learning you want; above all, the learner has to understand them [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Standards describe the desired knowledge, behavior or skill in specific terms, with conditions and criteria. When a learner performs to a well-defined standard, learning is evident. Standards are easy to write for the cognitive and psychomotor domains and harder for attitudes [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. When you list the criteria for an objective, you have already written the completion standards for the lesson plan [[25:110|AIH 5-7]], and clear objectives give the learner the big picture and remove a big source of uncertainty and frustration [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

callout.text: Do not stop at the minimum published standard. Professional instructors teach not only how, but also why and when, and build ADM and risk management into every lesson [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Lesson completion standards should gradually reach or exceed the ACS before final checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

body.p: Performance-based objectives. These set measurable, reasonable standards for the learner's performance, and may also be called behavioral, performance, instructional or educational objectives [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. They must be clear, measurable and repeatable, and mean the same thing to any knowledgeable reader [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. They have three elements [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]:

head: Element
What it is
Example from the AIH
rows: Description of the skill or behavior
The desired outcome in concrete, measurable terms. Avoid phrases like "knowledge of" or "awareness of" [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]
"Able to select from a list of" or "able to repeat the steps to" [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]
Conditions
The rules for showing the skill: equipment, tools, reference material and limits. If a reader asks "But what if...?", the conditions need work [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]
"Using appropriate charts, a prepared flight log, and training aircraft... while maintaining standard hemispheric altitudes" [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]
Criteria
The standards that measure success, so nobody can argue whether the objective was met [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]
Arrive within 5 minutes of planned time and hold cruise altitude within 200 feet [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]

body.p: Importance of the Airman Certification Standards (ACS) in aviation training curricula. The ACS give you specific performance objectives based on the standards for a certificate or rating, and the FAA reviews them often to keep them current [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. Test items should be content valid (the maneuver closely mimics real flying, like recovering from a power-off stall) and criterion valid (the completion standards reflect acceptable standards in real flight) [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. The PHAK describes the ACS as an enhanced PTS that adds task-specific knowledge and risk management elements [[1:37|PHAK 1-22]], and the RMH says risk management training works better when it is tied to the knowledge, risk and skill requirements in the ACS [[30:59|RMH A-1]].

callout.text: The ACS is a testing document, not a teaching document [[25:160|AIH 8-2]] [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. Its standards cover only the most critical job tasks, so a certification test does not represent an entire training syllabus [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Use the maneuver-based ACS, but present its objectives in scenarios [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

body.p: Decision-based objectives. These are designed to develop judgment and ADM. Poor pilot decisions cause a significant share of all accidents and most fatal ones [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. Using dynamic, meaningful scenarios, you teach the learner to gather information and make informed, safe and timely decisions [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. Shift toward them as the learner reaches higher levels of performance; they suit scenario-based training and teach critical thinking such as risk management and ADM [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. They do not replace maneuver training: maneuvers that need repetition are still drilled, then built into realistic scenarios [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. Data cited by the AIH suggest SBT learners fly as well or better than maneuver-only learners and make better decisions [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

check.q: A syllabus objective says "The learner will have knowledge of VOR navigation." What is wrong with it, and how do you fix it?
check.a: "Knowledge of" cannot be measured well [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Rewrite it with a measurable description, the conditions (equipment, references, limits) and criteria that leave no doubt whether it was met [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

body.p: After the objectives and standards are set, you make a plan that leads learners logically to the goal, usually a certificate or rating, using a training syllabus [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]. The traditional organization of a lesson is introduction, development and conclusion [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

head: Part
What goes in it
Watch for
rows: Introduction: attention
Focus every learner on the lesson with a story, video clip, question or joke that relates to the subject [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]
A story or joke unrelated to the subject distracts from the lesson [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]
Introduction: motivation
Specific reasons the content matters, which ensures readiness (law of readiness). Use examples of someone applying it, or an upcoming assessment [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]
Make it appeal to each learner personally [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]
Introduction: overview
A clear, short statement of the objective and key ideas: a road map [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]
A good visual aid can show the path [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]
Development
The main part. Organize the material to show how the main points relate [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]
Subordinate points should lead naturally from one to the next [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]
Conclusion
Retrace the important elements and relate them to the objective. This review reinforces learning and retention [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]
Never introduce new ideas here; they confuse learners [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]

body.p: Four ways to develop the main points [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]:

bullets: Past to present: arrange material in time order when history matters, as in tracing radio navigation systems [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

Simple to complex: start with simple facts and build to the concept, like a toy balloon before a gas turbine engine. Leave out less important information at first: a learner who flies only in Class D, E and G airspace can wait for A, B and C [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].
Known to unknown: start from something the learner knows, like the magnetic compass before gyroscopic heading indicators [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].
Most frequently used to least used: begin with what everyone uses, like basic navigation before a computerized navigation system [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

body.p: Clear transitions between main points keep learners oriented about where they have been and where they are going, which helps them sort and remember the information [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Figure 5-6 is the AIH checklist for presenting a lesson [[25:111|AIH 5-8]]:

check.q: You open a lesson on airspace with a funny story about your college roommate. What is the problem?
check.a: The attention step should relate to the subject; an unrelated story or joke distracts from the lesson [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

chunks.title: Delivery methods: lecture, discussion and guided discussion

body.p: Training delivery methods include lecture, discussion, guided discussion, problem-based, group learning, demonstration-performance and e-learning. In a typical lesson an effective instructor uses a combination [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

Lecture. The instructor delivers knowledge to learners who are more or less silent. It is best for giving a general understanding and runs introduction, body, summary [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Lectures can introduce subjects, summarize, link theory to practice and work for small or large groups [[25:114|AIH 5-11]]. Kinds include the illustrated talk, the briefing, the formal lecture and the teaching lecture [[25:114|AIH 5-11]]. The teaching lecture is the one aviation instructors favor, because learners take some part; you read their reactions from faces and note-taking and adjust [[25:114|AIH 5-11]].

bullets: Prepare it in four steps: set the objective and desired outcomes, research the subject, organize the material, and plan productive classroom activities. Then rehearse, ideally with another instructor acting as critic [[25:114|AIH 5-11]].
Use simple words, define every technical term, and choose specific words: "a leak in the fuel line" says more than "discrepancy." Mix short and medium sentences [[25:115|AIH 5-12]].

Deliver it extemporaneously from an outline, not read or memorized, so you can expand a point when you see puzzled faces [[25:115|AIH 5-12]]. Use notes sparingly but do not hide them [[25:115|AIH 5-12]].

Strengths: many ideas in a short time, large groups, and common background for learners with varied experience [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. Weaknesses: no precise measure of understanding, retention drops after the first 10 to 15 minutes, and it does not build motor skills. Add active participation in the middle [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].

body.p: Discussion. A short lecture gives basic knowledge, followed by instructor-learner and learner-learner discussion [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. Keep it on the subject with leading questions, deal with disagreements, get everyone to take part and summarize. It builds higher order thinking skills (HOTS), and your own talking should be kept to a minimum [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].

Guided discussion. Used to make sure the learner has received and interpreted information correctly. Learners need some background first (reading or a short lecture), and the instructor keeps control. It works in the classroom and in preflight and postflight briefings [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. The goal is to draw out what the learner knows: treat everyone impartially, encourage questions, be patient and tactful, and never use sarcasm [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].

bullets: Questions do the work. Open with a lead-off question, steer with follow-up questions, and you may answer a question with a question [[25:117|AIH 5-14]]. Avoid yes or no and short factual questions; ask open-ended ones [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].

Plan at least one lead-off question for each desired outcome, usually starting with how or why. "Why does an aircraft normally need a longer takeoff run at Denver than at New Orleans?" starts a discussion; "Denver or New Orleans?" gets one word [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].

Give learners time to think, rephrase if they look puzzled, and use an interim summary after each outcome [[25:118|AIH 5-15]]. Close by tying the points to practical use, such as a density altitude accident [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].
Learners should not be asked to discuss a subject with no background; if there was no prework, give a brief general survey in the introduction [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].

callout.text: "What if?" questions in a guided discussion call for HOTS and expose the learner to decision making. As the learner grows, let them lead the postflight review while you guide with targeted questions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].

check.q: Turn "Is a high density altitude bad for takeoff performance?" into a good lead-off question.
check.a: Ask how or why, for example "Why does an aircraft need a longer takeoff run at Denver than at New Orleans?" Yes or no questions do not start a discussion [[25:117|AIH 5-14]] [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].

chunks.title: Delivery methods: group learning, demonstration-performance, drill and practice

body.p: Cooperative or group learning. Learners work in small groups to maximize understanding. Research shows better test scores, higher self-esteem, better social skills and greater comprehension, and it keeps everyone actively involved [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Success depends on conditions and controls, starting with clear, specific objectives for what each learner must be able to do alone [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]:

bullets: Small, heterogeneous groups, with clear and complete instructions on what to do, in what order, with what materials [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].
Learners see the objectives as their own, have the chance to succeed, and can get and understand the information they need [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].
Enough time, individual accountability, recognition for group success, and time afterward to reflect on how the team worked [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

body.p: Types include collaborative, learner-led, instructor-led and working groups, with you as coach or facilitator [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Bob uses it after his weight and balance lecture: groups solve the first problem, then each learner solves one alone [[25:104|AIH 5-1]].

Demonstration-performance. Best for mental or physical skills that need practice, it is based on the principle that people learn by doing [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Chapter 5 divides it into five phases: explanation, demonstration, learner performance, instructor supervision and evaluation [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Chapter 9 combines performance and supervision into one phase, since they happen at the same time [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

head: Phase
What you do
rows: Explanation

Clear, pertinent to the objective and based on what the learner already knows. Give the precise actions and the end result, and invite questions [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. In flight training it happens before the flight with objectives, completion standards, a thorough briefing and the safety procedures [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]
Demonstration
Show the actions, with nothing extra. If the demonstration departs from the explanation, say so and explain why right away [[25:125|AIH 5-22]]
Learner performance and instructor supervision

The learner performs while you supervise. Allow enough time and let them try as soon as possible after the demonstration; they may follow along on the controls first, then try it with coaching [[25:125|AIH 5-22]]
Evaluation

The learner works alone while you judge the performance against how it was taught; this also measures your instruction [[25:125|AIH 5-22]]. Point out what to improve with concrete suggestions, and avoid ending on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]

body.p: In flight, the AIH applies the method as the telling-and-doing technique. The key difference is the transition step, learner tells and instructor does, between your demonstration and the learner's practice [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. In the first step you demonstrate exactly the way the learner should practice, in the same order you explained it, including safety procedures [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

Drill and practice. Built on Thorndike's law of exercise: connections get stronger with practice. Nobody masters crosswind landings in one flight; learners improve each time they practice what they were told and shown. Your job is to give practice opportunities and keep them aimed at an objective [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].

check.q: During your demonstration of turns around a point a gust pushes you wide of the circle you described. What should you do?
check.a: Acknowledge the deviation and explain it right away, because the demonstration should match the explanation [[25:125|AIH 5-22]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

body.p: Problem-based learning (PBL) began in 1966 at the McMaster University School of Medicine and moved teaching from instructor-centered to learner-centered. The AIH defines it as lessons that involve learners with problems met in real life and ask them to find real-world solutions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]]. A PBL lesson starts with a carefully built problem that has no single solution; it deepens understanding, improves recall and develops HOTS [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].
Effective problems [[25:119|AIH 5-16]]:

bullets: Relate to the real world, so learners want to solve them.
Require learners to make decisions.
Are open-ended, not limited to one correct answer.
Connect to what was learned before as well as new knowledge.
Reflect the lesson objectives.
Challenge learners to think critically.

body.p: The AIH's basic approach to teaching HOTS through a problem: set up the problem; set learning outcomes for it; solve it; reflect on the process; consider other solutions through guided discovery; reevaluate with the new options; reflect on why this could be the best solution; and consider what "best" means [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

head: Type of problem-based instruction
How it works
Example
rows: Scenario-based training (SBT)

A highly structured script of real-world experiences in an operational setting. There may be no single right answer, so know in advance which outcomes are good or poor and let the learner make decisions without risking safety [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]
A flight scenario starts with a reason to fly: Mark is flying friends to a playoff game when clouds force him down to 1,000 feet with visibility down to 3 miles [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]
Collaborative problem-solving
You give a group a problem and help only when needed, since solving it without help is part of learning. One-on-one, you give limited help while the learner solves it [[25:121|AIH 5-18]]
Open-ended "what if" problems [[25:121|AIH 5-18]]
Case study
A real-life story the learners analyze to reach conclusions and possible solutions [[25:121|AIH 5-18]]
An NTSB accident description with the probable cause removed; the learners propose causes, then you share the NTSB's finding [[25:121|AIH 5-18]]

body.p: A problem-based lesson usually includes a reason to solve the problem, a decision on how to find a solution, a possible solution, an explanation of the reasoning, and reflection on it [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. SBT design (objectives, pre-scenario planning, good scenario traits) was covered in the Learning Process lesson; here the point is that SBT is one form of PBL [[25:120|AIH 5-17]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

check.q: How does the AIH suggest turning an NTSB report into a case study?
check.a: Remove the probable cause, let learners analyze the facts and suggest causes without bias, then share the NTSB's finding and discuss how to avoid that accident [[25:121|AIH 5-18]].

body.p: E-learning is an umbrella term for any education with an electronic part, from a stand-alone program that runs from lecture to exam to an interactive web course [[25:121|AIH 5-18]]. It is time flexible, cost competitive, learner-centered, easily updated and available anywhere [[25:121|AIH 5-18]]. Flight training devices and simulators, from desktop basic aviation training devices to airline simulators, are part of it [[25:121|AIH 5-18]]. Main advantages: learners feel in control, less time spent on instruction, and higher mastery and retention; distance learning connects learners who are far apart [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].

Limitations: little peer interaction or personal feedback, harder for you to control, good programs can be hard to find, the cost of equipment and software, and users who do not know a program well [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].

callout.text: Improper or excessive use: do not let a software program on traffic patterns and landings be the only ground instruction and then expect the learner to fly patterns and landings [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. Learners who rely heavily on electronic media are generally not as well trained as those who get a balanced mix of e-learning, class and one-on-one teaching [[25:172|AIH 9-2]].

bullets: Computer-assisted learning (CAL): a PC with multimedia software. Learners go at their own pace and time; test prep programs are one form [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].
The computer cannot tell when a learner is struggling, so you keep monitoring with supervision, questions, quizzes or guided discussion [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].

Simulation, role-playing and video gaming put the learner in a character's shoes facing a real-world problem and usually build critical thinking, but not every objective fits them [[25:123|AIH 5-20]].

Flight simulation devices come in three FAA categories: full flight simulators (FFS), flight training devices (FTD) and aviation training devices (ATD) [[25:172|AIH 9-2]]. ATDs cannot be used for airman practical tests [[25:173|AIH 9-3]].

check.q: A learner finished a CAL course on airspace with a high score. Can you skip checking what she learned?
check.a: No. The computer has no way of knowing when a learner is having difficulty; you remain responsible for monitoring progress with questions, quizzes or discussion [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].

body.p: Instructional aids are devices that help in teaching. They are not self-supporting: they support, supplement or reinforce what you teach. Training media is broader: any physical means of carrying the message, such as your voice, printed text, programs, part-task trainers or flight training devices [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

Characteristics of effective instructional aids. Well-chosen, well-organized visuals help learners understand and retain key information; aids should cover key points, be straightforward and factual, and simple ones are generally best [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. Figure 5-17 summarizes the qualities [[25:128|AIH 5-25]]:

bullets: They gain and hold attention, and sound plus sight uses the two most important senses, as long as the aid is not a distracting gimmick [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].
They improve retention: studies range from a 10 to 15 percent increase to as much as 80 percent [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].
They help with language barriers when the terms are chosen to mean the same thing to learner and instructor [[25:127|AIH 5-24]].
They clarify relationships, such as subsystems in a schematic or location, size and time on a graph [[25:127|AIH 5-24]].
They save time: play the sound or show the picture instead of describing it [[25:127|AIH 5-24]].

body.p: Guidelines for use. Plan each aid to support a specific point. Establish the objective, gather data, organize it into an outline or lesson plan, then pick the ideas that need an aid: long technical descriptions, complex points, places where you catch yourself forming a picture, or where learners look puzzled [[25:127|AIH 5-24]]. Keep aids simple and words to a minimum, and do not use them as a crutch or fill them with distracting artwork [[25:127|AIH 5-24]]. An aid that cannot be heard or seen has no value: test sound in the real room and make lettering big enough for the farthest learner [[25:128|AIH 5-25]]. Check a rough draft for accuracy, terminology, spelling and clarity [[25:128|AIH 5-25]].

Types. The most common and economical aids are marker boards and supplemental print material such as charts, diagrams and graphs. Others include projected material, video, computer-based programs, and models, mock-ups or cut-aways [[25:128|AIH 5-25]].

head: Type
Notes
rows: Marker board
Reusable and good for joint learner-instructor work [[25:128|AIH 5-25]]
Supplemental print material
Photos, drawings, charts, diagrams and graphs give a common visual image [[25:129|AIH 5-26]]
Enhanced training materials
Syllabi with endorsement and recordkeeping built in; maneuvers guides that include the ACS [[25:129|AIH 5-26]]
Projected material and video
Must be current and previewed; give an overview before and a summary after. Video does not replace the instructor [[25:129|AIH 5-26]]
Interactive systems and CAL
Software that branches on the user's choices; with CAL you become a facilitator but still control the learning [[25:129|AIH 5-26]] [[25:130|AIH 5-27]]
Models, mock-ups and cut-aways

A model copies a real object; a mock-up stands in for something too costly or dangerous; a cut-away shows the inside. If a two-dimensional picture does the job, use it, because models cost more [[25:130|AIH 5-27]]
Test preparation material
Stresses rote learning, the lowest level; use it only as a supplement to instructor-led training [[25:131|AIH 5-28]]

check.q: Your slide on the fuel system has a full paragraph of text and clip-art airplanes. Which guidelines does it break?
check.a: Words on an aid should be kept to a minimum and distracting artwork avoided; the aid should be simple and support a key point [[25:127|AIH 5-24]].

body.p: Integrated flight instruction teaches learners to fly maneuvers by both outside visual references and flight instruments. Instrument references start the first time each maneuver is introduced, and the control inputs are the same whichever reference is used [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. The AFH recommends this "integrated" or "composite" method when introducing basic maneuvers [[24:66|AFH 3-5]].

bullets: About 90 percent of attention goes outside to the natural horizon and to scanning for traffic [[24:66|AFH 3-5]].
The instruments confirm the attitude and performance; any correction is made with reference to the natural horizon, then rechecked [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
No more than about 10 percent of attention should be inside the flight deck [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

body.p: Why teach it this way: it builds early habits of instrument cross-check, interpretation and aircraft control, improves landings through better airspeed control, and gives better navigation and coordination [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Instrument-rated pilots have a much better safety record than pilots of similar time without instrument training [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Precise speeds, power and headings also improve climb and cruise performance [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], and the learner gains the ability to control the aircraft for limited periods if outside references are lost [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

How to teach it: start with the first briefing on the flight controls, covering both the instrument indications and the outside references. Introduce each new maneuver with both, and keep integrating them throughout; failing to do so lengthens the training needed for a private certificate [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

bullets: Common error: making pitch or bank corrections while still looking inside [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
Common error: fixating on the instruments and "chasing" them because of lag and precession. Instrument covers for the first hours can force the learner back outside [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

callout.text: Make sure learners understand that this introduction to instruments does not prepare them for marginal weather or IMC. VFR flight into IMC is one of the most common causes of fatalities [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Any time attitude cannot be kept by the natural horizon, it is a genuine emergency [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

body.p: Integrating ground and flight. Relate ground objectives to flight objectives and point out the link between theory and practice [[25:172|AIH 9-2]]. An integrated curriculum can run from classroom to simulator to airplane, as in the AIH's ILS example [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. Even after ground school, review the task with the learner before the flight [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]; paired ground and flight instruction moves learners further, faster [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

check.q: Your learner says, "Now that I can fly turns on instruments, I can handle a little cloud." How do you answer?
check.a: Integrated flight instruction does not prepare a pilot for marginal weather or IMC, and VFR into IMC is one of the most common causes of fatalities [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. It only gives limited control if outside references are lost [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

chunks.title: Planning instructional activity: blocks, syllabus and lesson plans

body.p: Chapter 7 plans instruction around four topics: course of training, blocks of learning, training syllabus and lesson plans [[25:145|AIH 7-1]].

Blocks of learning. Once the overall objectives are set, identify the blocks that make up the whole. Like a pyramid, some blocks never show on the surface, but each is needed; extra blocks are expensive frills, especially in flight [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]. Blocks should be fairly consistent in scope and be units you can measure, not a list of periods. A private course might be split into solo, solo cross-country and the certificate [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

Each finished block boosts confidence, and learners go from simple to complex: a normal landing before short-field and soft-field landings [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]. Learn the learner's background: a helicopter pilot moving to airplanes understands speed control but not how to get it in an airplane [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

Training syllabus. A brief but complete digest of the course, with blocks in the most efficient order, usually lesson by lesson and sometimes with recommended times [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Syllabi for approved schools follow 14 CFR parts 141 and 142; others may lack prerequisites, completion times and stage checks [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Use it as a guide: under part 61 the order can and should change for the learner's progress, weather, aircraft and schedule [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. When you depart from it, think about how the blocks relate. A learner struggling with normal landings might review slow flight before short-field landings are added [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. At a certificated school the approved syllabus is a condition of graduation [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Build in risk management for each stage, with more subtle risks as training goes on [[25:149|AIH 7-5]], and use it for recordkeeping [[25:150|AIH 7-6]].

Lesson plans. A lesson plan is an organized outline for one instructional period: what to do, in what order and by what procedure [[25:151|AIH 7-7]]. A mental outline is not a lesson plan. Write it down so another instructor could teach the same period from it [[25:151|AIH 7-7]]. An adequate plan selects material wisely and drops unimportant detail, gives each part its due, sets an efficient sequence, outlines the teaching procedure, relates the lesson to the course, gives a new instructor confidence, and keeps instruction uniform [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

head: Characteristic of a well-planned lesson
Meaning
rows: Unity
One unified segment with limited objectives [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]
Content
New material, related to the last lesson, usually with a short review [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]
Scope
Reasonable: too much confuses, too little is inefficient [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]
Practicality
Planned for where it happens, airplane or classroom, and the aids on hand [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]
Flexibility
Room to add material if needed [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]
Relation to course of training
Its link to the course objectives is clear to the learner [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]
Instructional steps
Follows preparation, presentation, application, and review and evaluation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]

body.p: Use it properly: know it well, use it as a guide, adapt it to the class or learner (in flight it may be modified or even abandoned for review), and revise it as aids, rules and manuals change [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Every format includes objectives, content and completion standards [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

With the traditional plan above, the learner can only practice the maneuver with help at the end [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. An SBT lesson plan for arriving at a specific nontowered airport ends with a learner who can describe a safe arrival at any nontowered airport in a range of winds [[25:155|AIH 7-11]].

callout.text: A flight instructor must sign the logbook of each person given flight or ground training. The instructor must also keep a record of the name of each person endorsed for solo (with the date) and of each person endorsed for a knowledge or practical test (with the kind of test, the date and the result), and keep those records at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189]]. The AIH adds a training folder for each learner, kept at least 3 years [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

check.q: A new CFI says, "I don't need to write lesson plans; I have them in my head." What does the AIH say?
check.a: A mental outline is not a lesson plan. It should be written so another instructor could conduct the same lesson and so it can be checked for completeness [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].

body.p: Your success depends largely on organizing the material and choosing a method that fits the lesson [[25:125|AIH 5-22]], and the setting and purpose decide which method to use [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. A wrong choice wastes time and money, and some mismatches leave real gaps in a pilot's skill.

head: Mismatch
What goes wrong
Better choice
rows: Lecture to teach a motor skill
Lecture does not build motor skills, which need hands-on practice [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
Demonstration-performance [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]
Long lecture with no participation
Retention drops after the first 10 to 15 minutes [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
Add active participation in the middle [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
Guided discussion on a subject the class knows nothing about
Learners cannot reach the outcomes without some background [[25:117|AIH 5-14]] [[25:118|AIH 5-15]]
Assign reading first, or give a brief general survey [[25:118|AIH 5-15]]
E-learning as the only ground training
The learner is expected to fly what was only seen on a screen [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]
A balanced mix of e-learning, class and one-on-one [[25:172|AIH 9-2]]
Test prep in place of teaching
Rote learning, the lowest level; learners pass the test but miss critical knowledge [[25:131|AIH 5-28]]
Use it only as a supplement [[25:131|AIH 5-28]]
Teaching to the ACS minimum
The ACS is a testing tool, not a teaching tool [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]
Teach why the standards exist and raise lesson standards toward the ACS [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]
Stalls taught in the airplane only
Progress is poorer than when stalls are also discussed on the ground [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]
Ground lesson, then flight [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]

body.p: Match the learner, too. No two learners are alike, so analyze each one's personality, thinking and ability and be ready to change methods [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]. Most new instructors copy their own instructor's methods; learning under a system does not prove it was the best way [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

bullets: A discouraged or slow learner: set easier goals and break the task into elements, such as S-turns with headings only at first [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].
A fast learner: keep raising the standard, but never invent deficiencies [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].
A plan that is not working with this class: change the approach [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

check.q: Your plan for a quiet, nervous learner calls for drilling fundamentals, but the problem is confidence. What does the AIH suggest?
check.a: Direct the instruction toward building self-confidence rather than drilling fundamentals [[25:159|AIH 8-1]], and set more easily attained goals broken into elements [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

chunks.title: How to build your two checkride lesson plans

body.p: The ACS asks you to prepare a lesson plan with methods and materials that fit the Task and the learner. Use the AIH planning cycle: set the objective, research the subject, choose the method, pick a format, organize the lesson and select support material, assemble aids, then write the outline. Writing the beginning and the ending first helps [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. Commercial lesson plans are acceptable on the practical test, but adapt them [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

Aeronautical knowledge ground lesson applicable for a classroom (S1a). Example only (application: this lesson's own sample, not an FAA plan): a density altitude lesson for a small class might look like this. The Source column shows where the AIH backs each part.

head: Part
What you write
Source
rows: Objective
A performance-based objective with description, conditions and criteria
Introduction
Attention (a related question or short video), motivation (why it matters to them) and an overview
Development
Simple to complex; a teaching lecture with questions, then a guided discussion that opens with "Why a longer takeoff run at Denver than at New Orleans?"
Application
Small groups work a problem together, then each learner solves one alone
Aids
Marker board and a chart, checked for accuracy and visible from the back row
Conclusion and assessment
Summarize with no new ideas, then have learners show they met the objective; completion standard like Figure 7-2's minimum 80 percent with every miss reviewed

body.p: Maneuver introduction and ground lesson (S1b). Example only (application: this lesson's own sample, not an FAA plan): a plan for turns around a point, built on Figure 7-6 and the demonstration-performance method.

head: Part
What you write
Source
rows: Objective and completion standards
Control wind drift within set limits of heading, altitude and airspeed; add a decision-based objective
Preflight discussion
Objective and standards, checklist, weather, safety procedures and positive exchange of flight controls
Review
Heading, speed, bank, altitude, terrain, wind direction and velocity
Explanation and demonstration plan
Instructor tells and does, in the same order you explained, using both outside and instrument references
Practice and supervision
Learner tells, then learner does, with coaching
Postflight
Learner self-assessment first, then yours; preview next lesson; study assignment

callout.text: Practice saying why you chose each method. The examiner wants to hear that you matched the method to the Task and the learner, for example demonstration-performance for a skill and guided discussion to check understanding [[25:124|AIH 5-21]] [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].

check.q: What three parts must every lesson plan format include?
check.a: Objectives, content to support them, and completion standards [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

body.p: These are planning and classroom errors the AIH warns about, and each one is easy for an examiner to spot in your lesson plan or presentation.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Unmeasurable objective
"Knowledge of" or "awareness of" in the objective [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]
State description, conditions and criteria [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]
Plan kept in your head
Points left out, the lesson drifts [[25:151|AIH 7-7]] [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]
Write it so another instructor could teach it [[25:151|AIH 7-7]]
Too much in one lesson
Confused learners [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]
Keep the scope reasonable [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]
New ideas in the conclusion
Learners leave confused [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]
Only retrace key points and tie them to the objective [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]
Reading the lecture word for word
No flexibility when learners look puzzled [[25:115|AIH 5-12]]
Speak extemporaneously from an outline [[25:115|AIH 5-12]]
Cluttered or unseen aids
Back row cannot read it; aid used as a crutch [[25:127|AIH 5-24]] [[25:128|AIH 5-25]]
Few words, large lettering, checked in the room first [[25:127|AIH 5-24]] [[25:128|AIH 5-25]]
Demonstration that does not match the explanation
Learner copies the wrong thing [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Demonstrate exactly as explained, or acknowledge the deviation [[25:125|AIH 5-22]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Following the plan no matter what
Learner lacks the basics the lesson needs [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]
Modify the plan, or abandon it for review [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]

check.q: In your conclusion you add "one more thing" about a topic you did not cover. Why is that a problem?
check.a: New ideas should not be introduced in the conclusion because they are likely to confuse the learners [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

scenario.title: Two lessons for a new instructor
scenario.setup: You have just been hired as a CFI at a part 61 school. On Monday you teach a 50-minute classroom lesson on weather briefings to five learner pilots, two of whom have not done any reading. On Tuesday you start flying with Alex, a commercial helicopter pilot adding an airplane rating. His last instructor left a note: "Taught traffic patterns with the simulator app only, no notes kept." Alex is struggling with normal landings, and the school syllabus says short-field landings come next. The school owns a projector, a marker board and an aviation training device.

questions.q: How would you open Monday's classroom lesson?
questions.a: With an introduction of attention, motivation and overview: a related story, video or question; specific reasons the topic matters to them; and a road map of the objective and key ideas [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

questions.q: You planned a guided discussion. What do you do about the two learners with no background?
questions.a: Learners should not discuss a subject with no background; give a brief general survey of the topic in the introduction [[25:118|AIH 5-15]], or start with a short lecture [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].

questions.q: You plan a 50-minute lecture with slides. What risk do you manage, and how?
questions.a: Retention drops after the first 10 to 15 minutes and lectures give no precise measure of understanding; build active participation into the middle [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. Keep slide words to a minimum [[25:127|AIH 5-24]] and preview the projected material beforehand [[25:129|AIH 5-26]].

questions.q: What does the previous instructor's note tell you about Alex's training?
questions.a: Software alone should not be relied on for traffic pattern and landing instruction [[25:122|AIH 5-19]], and missing records leave you unsure of his status; accurate records keep learner and instructor informed and support endorsements [[25:150|AIH 7-6]].

questions.q: Do you follow the syllabus and add short-field landings?
questions.a: No. The syllabus is a guide; when departing from it consider the blocks. Delay short-field landings and review slow flight so he can succeed and build the skills for normal landings [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. A normal landing comes before short-field and soft-field landings [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

questions.q: How does Alex's helicopter background change your plan?
questions.a: Plan blocks that build on what he knows: a helicopter pilot understands speed control but not how to get it in an airplane [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Analyze the learner and adapt your methods [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

skills.do: Prepare an instructional lesson plan using teaching methods and materials appropriate for Task and learner characteristics (ACS FI.I.C.S1). The examiner sees a written plan with objectives, content and completion standards, and hears you explain why each method and aid fits this Task and this learner.
skills.practice: Write plans with the planning cycle, beginning and end first [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. For each, list the method you chose and why (for example demonstration-performance for a skill [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]), and have another instructor critique a dry run [[25:114|AIH 5-11]].

skills.do: Aeronautical knowledge ground lesson applicable for a classroom (ACS FI.I.C.S1a). The examiner sees a classroom lesson with an introduction (attention, motivation, overview), organized development, a conclusion with no new ideas, and a way to check the objective was met.
skills.practice: Teach a 20-minute classroom topic to friends using a teaching lecture plus a guided discussion with a planned how or why lead-off question for each outcome [[25:118|AIH 5-15]]. Check your aids from the back of the room [[25:128|AIH 5-25]].

skills.do: Maneuver introduction and ground lesson (ACS FI.I.C.S1b). The examiner sees a preflight lesson on a maneuver: objective and completion standards, review, explanation with safety procedures, your demonstration plan and the learner practice plan.
skills.practice: Take a maneuver, write a plan on the Figure 7-6 pattern [[25:153|AIH 7-9]], add a decision-based objective [[25:110|AIH 5-7]], and rehearse the explanation phase out loud as you would before the flight [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

quiz.q: What are the four steps of the teaching process, in order?
options: Attention, motivation, overview, summary
Explanation, demonstration, performance, evaluation
Introduction, development, conclusion, review
Preparation, presentation, application, then assessment
quiz.why: The teaching process is preparation, presentation, application and assessment, whatever the delivery method [[25:104|AIH 5-1]].

quiz.q: Which is one of the four essential teaching skills named in the AIH?
options: Management skills
Aeronautical decision-making skills
Public speaking skills
Computer skills
quiz.why: The four are people skills, subject matter expertise, management skills and assessment skills [[25:104|AIH 5-1]].

quiz.q: Your syllabus is shifting toward decision-based objectives. What happens to maneuver training?
options: Maneuvers needing repetition are drilled, then built into scenarios
It is saved until after the checkride, when the scenarios are complete
It is dropped, since scenarios replace the repetition of maneuvers
It continues alone, and scenarios wait until the instrument rating
quiz.why: Decision-based objectives develop judgment and ADM, but they do not preclude traditional maneuver-based training. Maneuvers requiring repetition may still be taught in concentrated settings, and once learned they are integrated into realistic and dynamic flight situations [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

quiz.q: In the AIH, criterion validity of a test item means that:
options: The maneuver or task closely mimics what is done in actual flying
Its completion standards reflect acceptable standards in flight
Every examiner and instructor scores it the same way every time
It samples every objective in the whole training syllabus
quiz.why: Criterion validity means the completion standards reflect acceptable standards; content validity means the maneuver mimics actual flying [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

quiz.q: What three elements make up a lesson introduction?
options: Explanation, demonstration and practice
Attention, motivation and overview
Objective, content and standards
Review, preview and assignment
quiz.why: The introduction is made up of attention, motivation and an overview [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

quiz.q: Under part 61, your learner is struggling with normal landings, and the syllabus says short-field landings come next. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Add short-field landings on schedule, since the syllabus order is fixed
Stop all landing practice until the learner is ready for a stage check
Repeat normal landings every lesson with nothing else until they are perfect
Delay short-field landings and review slow flight to rebuild confidence
quiz.why: Under part 61 the syllabus is a guide, and its order can and should change to suit the learner's progress. When departing from it, consider how the blocks relate: the AIH example delays short-field landings and reviews slow flight, which lets the learner do well, regain confidence and build the skills for approaches and landings [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

quiz.q: Which is a condition for successful cooperative learning?
options: Small, heterogeneous groups
Large groups of similar learners
Grading only the group as a whole
Letting learners skip reflection
quiz.why: Small, heterogeneous groups, along with individual accountability and time to reflect, are listed conditions [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

quiz.q: Studies on instructional aids show retention gains ranging from:
options: 1 to 2 percent up to as much as 10 percent
A 10 to 15 percent increase up to as much as 80 percent
25 to 30 percent up to as much as 100 percent
No measurable gain
quiz.why: Results range from a 10 to 15 percent increase to as much as 80 percent [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

quiz.q: In integrated flight instruction, when should instrument references begin?
options: After the first solo
Only later, during instrument rating training
Only after the learner masters steep turns and stalls
The first time each new maneuver is introduced
quiz.why: For it to be fully effective, instrument references begin the first time each new maneuver is introduced [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

options: A sequence of class periods of equal length
Separate subjects with no link to each other
Units of learning that can be measured and evaluated
Added freely, since extra blocks cost nothing
quiz.why: Blocks should be consistent in scope and represent measurable units of learning, not a sequence of periods; extra blocks are expensive frills [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: A learner transfers to you from another school mid-course. Which instructional aid makes it easiest to see where her training stands?
options: A video library that shows every maneuver she will fly in the course
A test preparation app that tracks her practice test scores
A cut-away engine model of the school's training airplane
An enhanced syllabus with endorsement and training recordkeeping provisions
final_quiz.why: Enhanced syllabi with recordkeeping let the training record be reviewed and the training status easily assessed when a learner transfers to another school or instructor [[25:129|AIH 5-26]].

final_quiz.q: You planned a guided discussion on fronts, but the class did no reading and there was no time to assign any. What should you do?
options: Run the discussion anyway; they will learn from each other
Cancel the lesson
Give a brief general survey of the topic in the introduction
Switch to a written test
final_quiz.why: Learners should not discuss a subject without background; with no prework, give a brief general survey in the introduction [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].

final_quiz.q: Halfway through your teaching lecture, several learners look puzzled. What does extemporaneous delivery let you do?
options: Continue at the planned pace and take all their questions at the end
Read the next section of notes more slowly
Assign the material as homework
Elaborate on the point until their reactions show they understand
final_quiz.why: Speaking from an outline rather than reading lets you elaborate when puzzled expressions show learners did not grasp an idea [[25:115|AIH 5-12]].

final_quiz.q: A transfer learner did all her traffic pattern ground training with a software program and nothing else. What is the concern?
options: None; e-learning gives higher retention
Software cannot be logged
Improper or excessive use of e-learning
She needs a full flight simulator instead
final_quiz.why: A flight instructor should not rely exclusively on a program on patterns and landings for ground instruction and then expect the learner to fly them [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].

final_quiz.q: Which objective best meets the AIH standard for a performance-based objective?
options: Using a sectional chart, the learner will understand the airspace along a planned route
The learner will appreciate the importance of airspace and of staying out of Class B without a clearance
During the preflight briefing, the learner will have awareness of VFR weather minimums for each airspace class
Using a sectional chart, the learner will identify the airspace on a planned route with no errors
final_quiz.why: It states a measurable behavior, the conditions and criteria; "understand," "knowledge of" and "awareness of" cannot be measured well [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

final_quiz.q: Your school runs a learning center where an aide supervises learners on computer stations. What is your responsibility as the instructor?
options: Set procedures to ensure the training is done, since you certify competency
None; the aide who supervises the computer stations is responsible for it
Only grade the final exam, since the software tracks everything else
Review the software once a year and leave daily supervision to the aide
final_quiz.why: The responsible instructor must establish procedures to ensure the training is accomplished, because he or she certifies competency at the end [[25:130|AIH 5-27]].

final_quiz.q: A learner breezed through the knowledge test with a test prep app but cannot explain basic answers in your oral. What best explains it?
options: He is in the cognitive stage of skill learning
The knowledge test is too easy
Test prep material emphasizes rote learning
The app was out of date
final_quiz.why: Test prep material emphasizes rote learning, the lowest level; examiners report applicants who pass the test but lack knowledge in the oral [[25:131|AIH 5-28]].

final_quiz.q: Your plan for a learner with 4 hours covers stalls, steep turns, slow flight, emergency descents and ground reference maneuvers in one flight. Which characteristic of a well-planned lesson does it break?
options: Unity
Scope
Practicality
Flexibility
final_quiz.why: Each lesson should be reasonable in scope; a person can master only a few skills at a time, and too much material results in confusion [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

final_quiz.q: After integrated instruction, your learner loses the horizon in haze and cannot hold attitude visually. How should he have been taught to view this?
options: As a genuine emergency, since this training does not prepare him for IMC
As a reason to descend low until he can see the ground and hold attitude
As a routine instrument exercise, since he has practiced turns on instruments
As a time to rely on the autopilot alone until the haze clears
final_quiz.why: Anytime attitude cannot be kept by the natural horizon it is a genuine emergency, and integrated instruction does not prepare pilots for IMC [[24:67|AFH 3-6]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: You want to explain how a fuel system works and are deciding between a cut-away model and a printed diagram. If the diagram shows everything you need, which should you use?
options: The cut-away, because a three-dimensional model is always the better aid
Neither; describe it in words so learners build their own mental picture
The diagram; a two-dimensional aid that meets the need should be used
Both, every time, since more aids always mean better retention
final_quiz.why: Production and equipment costs limit models; if a two-dimensional representation satisfies the requirement, use it [[25:130|AIH 5-27]].

final_quiz.q: You want learners to analyze a real accident and reach their own conclusions without being swayed by the official finding. Which method fits?
options: Drill and practice on the accident's key facts
Case study with the NTSB probable cause removed
A formal lecture on the official NTSB findings
Test preparation software with accident questions
final_quiz.why: Removing the NTSB probable cause turns the report into a case study learners can discuss without bias; then share the finding [[25:121|AIH 5-18]].

final_quiz.q: A learner can fly every maneuver to ACS standards, so a colleague says your lessons should stop at the ACS. What does the AIH say?
options: Agree; the ACS lists everything a safe pilot needs to be taught
The ACS is a testing document, not a complete training syllabus
The ACS replaces lesson plans once the learner meets its standards
Only part 141 schools may train beyond what the ACS requires
final_quiz.why: The ACS is a testing document, not a teaching document [[25:160|AIH 8-2]], and its standards cover only the most critical tasks, not the whole syllabus [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

final_quiz.q: Ten minutes into a lesson on ground reference maneuvers, it is clear your learner cannot yet hold altitude in medium-bank turns, which the lesson depends on. What does the AIH say about your lesson plan?
options: End the flight and write a new plan before you fly again
Follow it as written, since a plan keeps the lesson orderly and complete
Modify it, or even abandon it in favor of review
Finish the planned maneuvers, then add the turns next week
final_quiz.why: A flight lesson plan should fit the learner's background, experience and ability. It may have to be modified considerably during flight because of deficiencies in the learner's knowledge or poor mastery of elements essential to the lesson, and in some cases the entire plan may have to be abandoned in favor of review [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

takeaways: Teaching runs in four steps: preparation, presentation, application and assessment.
Write objectives you can measure: description, conditions and criteria, then add decision-based objectives.
The ACS supplies performance objectives but is a testing document, not a whole syllabus.
Organize every lesson as introduction (attention, motivation, overview), development and conclusion.
Pick the delivery method for the lesson and the learner, and usually combine several.
Aids support you; keep them simple, visible and accurate, and never let software or test prep replace teaching.
Build courses from blocks, use the syllabus as a flexible guide, and put every lesson plan in writing.
cfi_notes: The AIH text puts "[Figure 5-1]" after the four teaching steps, but Figure 5-1 shows the four essential skills (people, subject matter, management, assessment) [[25:104|AIH 5-1]] [[25:105|AIH 5-2]]. If an examiner quotes the figure, know both lists.

The fourth step has three names in the AIH: assessment [[25:104|AIH 5-1]], review and evaluation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]], and evaluation in the demonstration-performance column of Figure 9-7 [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. They mean the same thing.

The PHAK still calls the test standard the PTS when it says it is a testing document and not a training syllabus [[1:37|PHAK 1-22]]; the AIH says the same of the ACS [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. Teach it with the ACS name.

The AIH recommends a training folder (lesson plans, training received, part 61 requirements met, solo endorsements) kept at least 3 years [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. That is good practice, not the rule. The legal minimum is 14 CFR 61.189: sign the logbook of each person you train, and record the name and date of each solo endorsement and the name, kind of test, date and result of each knowledge or practical test endorsement, kept at least 3 years [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189]]. Teach the CFR list as the requirement.
Commercially developed lesson plans are acceptable on the practical test [[25:153|AIH 7-9]], but bring plans you have adapted and can defend; the examiner will ask why you chose each method.

SBT is a type of problem-based instruction in the AIH [[25:120|AIH 5-17]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. If asked about problem-based instruction, name all three types: SBT, collaborative problem-solving and case study.
For a one-on-one learner, guided discussion and collaborative problem-solving both work; the AIH notes each can be modified for one-on-one teaching [[25:119|AIH 5-16]] [[25:121|AIH 5-18]].
Rehearse classroom lessons with another instructor as critic, and critique your own lesson afterward by noting what went well and what to improve [[25:114|AIH 5-11]] [[25:111|AIH 5-8]].
gaps: No source sets a required lesson plan format or length; the AIH notes that terms vary and that completion standards may be called assessment, review and feedback, or performance evaluation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].
The AIH points to AC 61-136 for ATD approval and credit [[25:173|AIH 9-3]], but that AC is not in this course's reference set. Check the current AC and the device's letter of authorization.
The sources give no time limit for a classroom lesson; Figure 7-2 itself does not specify time or number of periods [[25:148|AIH 7-4]].
The 10 to 15 percent and 80 percent retention figures are given without the studies behind them [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]; use them as illustrations.

The PHAK and RMH say little about lesson design: the PHAK urges a well-documented syllabus [[1:34|PHAK 1-19]] [[1:38|PHAK 1-23]] and the RMH ties risk management training to the ACS [[30:59|RMH A-1]]. Nearly all of this Task comes from the AIH.

activities.title: True or false: aids and e-learning
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Instructional aids are self-supporting and can stand in for your explanation.
cards.why: False. Instructional aids are not self-supporting; they support, supplement or reinforce what is taught [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

cards.s: Words on a visual aid should be kept to a minimum.
cards.why: True. Aids are used with a verbal presentation, so words on the aid should be kept to a minimum [[25:127|AIH 5-24]].

cards.s: A training video is designed to replace the instructor for that topic.
cards.why: False. The presentation is not designed to replace the instructor, who should summarize and answer questions [[25:129|AIH 5-26]].

cards.s: If a two-dimensional representation meets your need, use it instead of a model.
cards.why: True. Costs limit models, mock-ups and cut-aways, so use a two-dimensional representation when it satisfies the requirement [[25:130|AIH 5-27]].

cards.s: An aviation training device (ATD) can be used for an airman practical test.
cards.why: False. ATDs cannot be used for airman practical tests or type rating training requirements [[25:173|AIH 9-3]].

cards.s: In computer-assisted learning the computer will tell you when a learner is struggling.
cards.why: False. The computer has no way of knowing when a learner is having difficulty; monitoring stays your job [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].

activities.title: Numbers in objectives and attention
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: In integrated flight instruction no more than about 10 percent of attention goes inside. In one minute of flight, how many seconds is that at most?
An objective uses the AIH criterion of arriving within 5 minutes of planned time. The planned en route time is 72 minutes. What is the longest en route time that still meets it?
items.why: 72 + 5 = 77 minutes, from the AIH example criterion of 5 minutes [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

items.q: The same objective requires cruise altitude within 200 feet. Cruise is 5,500 feet. What is the lowest altitude that still meets it?
items.why: 5,500 - 200 = 5,300 feet, from the AIH example criterion of 200 feet [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

items.q: A ground lesson's completion standard is a minimum passing score of 80 percent, as in Figure 7-2. An exercise has 25 questions. How many must be correct?
You endorse a learner for a practical test in 2026. Until at least what year must you keep that record?
items.why: Records must be kept for at least 3 years: 2026 + 3 = 2029 [[60:344|14 CFR 61.189]].

activities.title: Planning Jamie's stall lessons, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are the CFI for Jamie, a learner pilot with 12 hours, about to start slow flight and stalls.

steps.s: You are planning how Jamie will first learn stalls.
options: Go straight to the airplane to save money
Ground lesson on stall types and aerodynamics, then the flight
Assign a test prep app and fly
Show a video and skip the briefing
steps.why: Learning stalls through flight instruction only gives poorer progress than also discussing them on the ground [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]; test prep stresses rote learning [[25:131|AIH 5-28]] and video does not replace the instructor [[25:129|AIH 5-26]].

steps.s: Twenty minutes into your ground explanation of stall aerodynamics, Jamie stops taking notes and looks glazed.
options: Bring Jamie in with questions or a short task
Speed up to finish the outline
End the lesson early
Keep talking; the material is important
steps.why: Retention drops after the first 10 to 15 minutes of a lecture, and active participation in the middle greatly increases retention [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. Read subtle signs like note-taking and adjust [[25:114|AIH 5-11]].

steps.s: In the airplane you are about to demonstrate the first power-off stall.
options: Let Jamie try first
Show a different variation to keep it interesting
Combine it with a steep turn to save time
Demonstrate it exactly as explained, in the same order, including safety procedures
steps.why: Learners imitate the instructor, so demonstrate exactly as they should practice, in the order explained, with all safety procedures [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

steps.s: Two lessons later Jamie's normal landings are poor and the syllabus calls for short-field landings next.
options: Skip ahead to cross-country planning
Proceed with short-field landings
Delay short-field landings and review slow flight
Tell Jamie to study more and repeat the same lesson unchanged
steps.why: Consider the blocks when departing from the syllabus; slow flight review rebuilds confidence and the skills for landings [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

steps.s: Back on the ground, Jamie still needed your help to recover from the power-off stall, so the lesson's completion standard was not met.
options: Sign the lesson off anyway so Jamie stays on schedule
Critique the performance, record it, plan more training on stalls, preview the next lesson and give a study assignment
Say nothing about it so Jamie stays motivated
Skip stalls and move on to the next block
steps.why: When a learner cannot meet the lesson's proficiency level in the time allotted, be ready to schedule additional training [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. The instructor evaluates and records the performance [[25:176|AIH 9-6]], and the traditional plan's postflight discussion is a critique, a preview of the next lesson and a study assignment [[25:154|AIH 7-10]].
